I am also skeptical of "soft sciences," which gets interesting when my chemist brother calls biology a "soft science" (I kick his ass ;P). I try not to be too judgmental though. Some studies are just entertaining reads. Unfortunately a lot of studies do have a big impact on how people are treated and cared for, so not very entertaining if they aren't reporting reliable info. I think with all papers you have to be cautious, read and interpret carefully, and consider it in light of larger bodies of evidence. It has been mentioned a lot in this sub, and I would agree, that self-reporting is probably the largest (necessary?) evil for many psychology studies. I don't think there is much way around it though. The only thing you can really do to try to counter it is carefully design the study and increase your sample size. I've seen psych papers that have n=40 or some crazy low number that basically indicated they asked their classmates. To get a good representation of a population, you should be required to sample at least 500 people. There should be some cut-off except in exceptional cases such as rare diseases/disorders. Even looking within a population, you have to either be really broad, or really specific. Being really specific costs less and lowers your sample size, but it probably isn't going to give you a good "big picture" look.
